title: The world has a new plan to save nature, but it still needs the money
gist: The COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan acknowledged the world will miss its 2030 Kunming-Montreal conservation goals and agreed a 'Yerevan Pathway' to accelerate action, but finance remains the key gap. About $2 billion in new pledges (including $500M from the Netherlands to Brazil's Tropical Forest Forever Facility) contrasts with a $200B/yr pledge and a 27% drop in environmental funding for 2026-30.

insights.claim: Leaders at COP17 in Yerevan recognized that conservation efforts are too slow to realistically achieve the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework goals of protecting about a third of land and seas by 2030.
insights.speaker: Financial Times

insights.claim: The Yerevan Pathway commits to tackling nature-harmful subsidies, increasing support for developing countries, and strengthening monitoring and reporting ahead of the next summit in Ecuador in two years.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Policy pressure on harmful subsidies may grow.
insights.locator: A plan was agreed to accelerate

insights.claim: Finance remains one of the biggest obstacles, and a fund for companies profiting from genetic materials to contribute voluntarily stands largely empty.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Voluntary corporate contribution mechanisms are failing.

insights.claim: Funding falls far short of the 2022 deal's pledge; Fauna & Flora argues the world can afford $200 billion a year for nature.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Large financing gap persists for conservation.
insights.quote: In a world of trillionaires, we can certainly afford to spend $200 billion a year on protecting and restoring the very thing keeping us all alive: nature

insights.claim: Close to $2 billion in new commitments were announced around the summit, including a $500 million Dutch pledge to Brazil's Tropical Forest Forever Facility.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: New pledges are two orders of magnitude below the stated need.
insights.locator: This included a commitment by the Netherlands

insights.claim: International environmental funding is set to decline 27 percent for 2026-30, driven by war disruption and high energy prices.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Geopolitical and energy shocks are crowding out conservation budgets.
insights.quote: with a 27 percent decline in environmental funding for the 2026-30 period

insights.claim: The Dutch pledge followed Lula's re-election as Brazil's president, which relieved many summit attendees given his record of protecting the Amazon.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Brazilian political continuity supports forest-finance mechanisms.
insights.locator: This included a commitment by the Netherlands

insights.claim: More countries drawing up national biodiversity plans and the new Brazilian fund pledge are reasons for cautious optimism, per Campaign for Nature.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Incremental progress amid a funding shortfall.
